home.headline: A can of cola leaves your stomach in about half an hour. A burger with fries can take four.
home.lead: LifePeek shows why. Pick two meals and watch them travel through the body side by side — how fast each leaves the stomach, where the sugar, protein, fat and fibre go, and how blood sugar responds.
home.previewCaption: Food still in the stomach after eating — computed by the LifePeek model

how.title: How it works
how.computed: Nothing is typed in by hand
how.computedBody: Each food is described by its nutrients and glycemic index, taken from published tables. The model works out how fast it leaves the stomach and how blood sugar responds.
how.honestBody: People differ. Times in the intestines and blood sugar are shown as typical ranges for healthy adults, with the source for every input.
how.classBody: Projector mode, English and Hindi, a step-by-step text view, works offline once loaded, and a link that reopens the exact same comparison.

mouth.name: Mouth
mouth.what: Teeth cut and grind food while the tongue mixes it with saliva into a soft ball called a bolus.
mouth.chemistry: Salivary amylase starts breaking starch into smaller sugars. Lingual lipase begins on fat, but very little happens yet.
mouth.fact: Your salivary glands make roughly 1 to 1.5 litres of saliva a day.

esophagus.name: Food pipe (oesophagus)
esophagus.what: Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, push each swallow down to the stomach in a few seconds.
esophagus.chemistry: No digestion happens here. Mucus helps the bolus slide.
esophagus.fact: Peristalsis works even upside down — astronauts can swallow in space.

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.what: The stomach stores the meal, churns it with acid into a thick liquid called chyme, and lets it out a little at a time through the pyloric sphincter.
stomach.chemistry: Hydrochloric acid unfolds proteins and kills many microbes. Pepsin starts cutting proteins into shorter chains. Liquids leave first; solids must be ground to tiny pieces before they can leave.
stomach.absorbed: Very little — some water, alcohol and a few drugs.
stomach.fact: The more calories a meal has, the more slowly it leaves: the small intestine signals the stomach to deliver only a few calories per minute.

smallIntestine.name: Small intestine
smallIntestine.what: Chyme moves through about 6 metres of narrow tube. Its lining is folded into millions of villi that give it a huge surface for absorption.
smallIntestine.chemistry: Bile from the liver breaks fat into tiny droplets. Pancreatic enzymes — amylase, lipase, trypsin — and enzymes on the villi finish breaking food into sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.
smallIntestine.absorbed: Most nutrients and most of the water are absorbed here into the blood and lymph.
smallIntestine.fact: The villi and microvilli give the small intestine a surface area of around 30 square metres — about half a badminton court.

largeIntestine.name: Large intestine
largeIntestine.what: What could not be digested — mainly fibre — moves slowly through the colon and is stored until it leaves the body.
largeIntestine.chemistry: Gut bacteria ferment fibre, making gases and short-chain fatty acids that feed the colon’s own cells. Some vitamins, such as vitamin K, are made by bacteria here.
largeIntestine.absorbed: Most of the remaining water and salts.
largeIntestine.fact: This is the slowest part of the journey: commonly a day or more.

disclaimer.short: Educational model of a typical healthy adult. Not medical advice.
disclaimer.long: LifePeek is a simplified teaching model. Times and blood-sugar values are typical ranges for healthy adults and vary a lot between people. It must not be used to make health, diet or medical decisions.

teach.title: Using LifePeek in class
teach.lead: LifePeek is built for a projector and a 40-minute lesson on nutrition and digestion (for example, the “Life Processes” chapter).
steps: Ask the class to predict: which leaves the stomach first — a can of cola or a burger with fries? Which raises blood sugar more?
Open the cola vs burger comparison and press Play. Pause when the cola is mostly out of the stomach and ask why.
Switch to Step by step and read the stomach stage together. Link the result to calories and fat.
Let groups build their own comparisons on their phones (no login needed) and share the link with you.
Close with the blood sugar chart: why does adding fat or protein flatten the curve?
questions: Why do drinks leave the stomach before solid food?
Fibre is never absorbed. Where does it end up, and what eats it?
Why is blood sugar shown as a band instead of one number?
Roti and dal versus white rice: which gives a gentler blood sugar curve? Look at each food’s glycemic index on the Science page.
tips: Turn on Projector mode for stronger contrast in a bright room.
Open the app once on Wi-Fi; after that it works offline.
Every comparison has its own link — save it in your notes to reopen the exact setup.
Use the Step by step view for students using screen readers or old phones.

science.title: Science and sources
science.lead: What the model computes, what it assumes, and where every number comes from.
science.modelBody: Stomach emptying is computed from the meal. Drinks start leaving straight away — water within minutes, drinks with calories at about 2 kcal per minute. Solid food is first ground for about 20 minutes, then leaves at about 1.4 kcal per minute, so meals with more calories take longer. (In the model a bigger meal empties at the same rate; real stomachs speed up a little for big meals.) Blood sugar is computed from the carbohydrate being absorbed, its glycemic index, and the slowing effect of fat and protein.
science.fixedBody: Time in the small and large intestine varies far more between people than between meals, so LifePeek uses typical published values and shows the range.
limits: Models a healthy adult only — not children, pregnancy, diabetes or digestive illness.
Blood sugar is a typical shape, not a prediction for any one person.
Exercise, sleep, stress and drinks with the meal all change real results.
Glycemic index values for mixed and home-cooked dishes vary between studies.
Fibre isn't modelled on its own: its slowing effect on blood sugar shows up through each food's glycemic index.
